Trump has been a criminal from the very beginning. Don't take my word for it—look into his history. Go back to 1976, long before the golden escalators, long before the White House, long before the red hats and the rallies. Go back to the Commodore Hotel scandal, where a young, hungry, and ruthless Donald Trump learned the first and most important lesson of his life: the law is not a wall—it's a door. And cash is the key.

He didn't have the money to buy the Commodore. So he didn't. He bought the politicians instead. He poured cash into their campaigns, and in return, they handed him a 40-year tax break—the largest in the history of New York City. That was his first masterpiece. That was the moment he realized that the system wasn't designed to stop people like him. It was designed to be rented by people like him.

And he never stopped. From the Commodore to Trump Tower—where he hired undocumented Polish workers, paid them pennies, and threatened them with deportation if they complained—to the casinos of Atlantic City, where he openly admitted that he bribed both parties because "that's the system." He said it himself. He bragged about it. And no one stopped him.

Then came Trump University—a fake school that stole $35,000 from desperate people who believed his name meant something. When the Florida Attorney General started investigating, his charity—illegally—cut her campaign a check for $25,000. The investigation vanished. The case was buried. And the victims? They were left with nothing.

This is not a politician. This is not a president. This is a predator who has spent five decades learning exactly how to exploit every crack, every loophole, every blind spot in the American system. He didn't break the law—he mastered it. He weaponized it. He turned it into a shield for himself and a sword against everyone else.
